forces: Orchestra; arrangement attributed to Karl Müller-Berghaus
intro: Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra play Liszt’s Second Hungarian Rhapsody in Karl Müller-Berghaus’s orchestral arrangement. This opening side of their 1936 recording turns the piano’s slow declamation into a public speech.

cues.title: A slow orchestral summons
cues.text: The Lassan, Liszt’s slow first half, begins with a brief introduction before settling into its minor key. Grave phrases alternate with lighter turns. In this arrangement, the orchestra takes over the changing characters of the piano original.
cues.evidence: The Lassan’s introduction and contrasting character are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2. The recording source attributes the arrangement to Müller-Berghaus: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PDP-CH_-_Philadelphia_Orchestra_-_Stokowski_-_Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2_in_C-sharp_minor,_S_244-2_-_Liszt_-_Hmv-db3086-2a03100.flac.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Three scores, three keys
cues.text: The piano original’s home key is C♯ minor. Liszt’s orchestral version, made with Franz Doppler, moves it up to D minor; Müller-Berghaus takes it down to C minor.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard distinguishes the piano original, Liszt–Doppler orchestration in D minor and Müller-Berghaus arrangement in C minor: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9. The selected recording’s attribution comes from its Commons description.

cues.title: Stokowski puts down the baton
cues.text: Late in the 1929–30 season, Stokowski begins conducting without a baton. In Philadelphia he experiments with seating, bowing and even the lights: at one concert only his head and hands are illuminated in the darkened hall.
cues.evidence: Stokowski’s free-hand conducting, orchestral experiments and concert lighting are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Stokowski, under Philadelphia Orchestra. The lighting episode is biographical, separate from this recording session.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: He could fit an orchestra under ten fingers, then end a lifetime at the piano with a few notes left hanging in the air.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces; no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked. A single pianist had taken possession of an entire evening.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained Liszt’s homeland, though German and French were the languages he used most easily. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano; Antonio Salieri taught him composition. Paris followed in 1823, but its Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. Private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha, continued his education.
